messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Time periods file
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Time periods file
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- various issues --

A. prt(tr) will just print a "tree table" to the screen.  It doesn't change anything about the analysis setup.  The point of doing "prt(tr)" is that you can then look at the node age column of this table to see exactly how old various nodes are. More on prt(): http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#prt

Of course, "tr" will have to be an APE tree object that you have already loaded.  The standard method is:

library(ape)
tr = read.tree(file="Put_your_newick_filename_here")

B. However... the STOP ERROR you got also tells you the age of your root node.  It says it is "33182.5346672406".  This suggests you have bigger problems!

This is because tree branch lengths are usually in millions of years, and since the Earth is only 4600 million years old, a tree age of 33182 my seems a bit high.

C. Always make sure you understand your basic phylogeny, how you got it, and whether or not it makes sense, before embarking on other analyses built on top of it.

I would recommend that you:

C1. Open your tree in FigTree, turn on the axis to see the timescale, and decide if your tree is looking like it should.

C2. I would recommend putting your tree in units of millions of years -- the BioGeoBEARS default parameters and min/max limits assume this kind of timescaling.  You can multiply or divide all of the branchlengths in your tree like this:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#manually_change_tree_length

C3. Read everything here:

Common BioGeoBEARS Mistakes To Avoid
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid

D. Once you've got a dated phylogeny you are happy with, you can address the STOP ERROR you got.

Let's say your tree was actually 3.3 my old (ie, the root node has an age of 3.3 my), and you had 2 areas, A and B

Then, these files would give your STOP ERROR:

timeperiods.txt
==================
1
2
3
==================

manual_dispersal_multipliers.txt
==================
A B
1.0 1.0
0.5 1.0

A B
1.0 1.0
0.3 1.0

A B
1.0 1.0
0.1 1.0

END

==================

But, these files would fix it:

timeperiods.txt
==================
1
2
3
4
==================

manual_dispersal_multipliers.txt
==================
A B
1.0 1.0
0.5 1.0

A B
1.0 1.0
0.3 1.0

A B
1.0 1.0
0.1 1.0

A B
1.0 1.0
0.9 1.0

END

==================

The file formats and example files are all explained here:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#links_to_files

...they make more sense if you read Ree & Smith (2008), Systematic Biology, first, since the example files are based on their example dataset, Hawaiian Psychotria.

Cheers,
Nick

Hi all,

It took some doing, but I think I figured out a hack that will fix the plotting issue under APE 5.0, but leave the plotting the same as before for versions of APE before 5.0.

I just ran the example script and the issue is fixed, and the plots plot without errors.  (However, now I see that the tip labels -- species names -- are offset to the right more than in previous plots.  I will wait awhile to work on this one as it is not crucial, and might change back if they change something else in APE.)

To get the update, just re-run the source command for the plotting code:

source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")

I ran the example Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping (BSM) script also and that seems to work fine also.  But, let me know if people find errors elsewhere after they upgrade to APE 5.0.

Cheers!
Nick

Nick, I am doing both an area and a biome analysis on a set of 528 species. BSM under DEC+J for the area data works fine. BAYAREALIKE modified with a+ and both d and e = 0 (no j either) works fine to get a resulting set of pdfs. However, BSM applied under the same conditions has issues. Trying to do 100 max runs, but many of them fail, even when maxtries is set to 4 million. The tips are more polymorphic with the biome than area dataset. This is a typical error message:

Error in stochastic_map_branch(): Stochastic mapping failed after maxtries=4e+06 tries on branch below node=5

As manual_history_for_difficult_branches==TRUE, we are manually devising a history to force-fit a difficult branch (e.g. AB -> ACEDFGH)...

NOTE: This fix will run, but will NOT work correctly for pure '+a' models (as of 2016-05-07) where d and/or e equals 0, since the manual fix forces a random series of d and e events, on the theory that the events must be super-rare since maxtries failed, so we might as well order them randomly (subject to the constraint that the range is never NULL). For +a models, try increasing maxtries instead.

Starting range:  BC

Desired ending range:  BG

When the run does complete and I try to summarize the results, the file often has just a few runs saved even though many more succeeded as they flashed across the screen. Your Dupin et al. 2017 paper ends with this comment "While implemented models are currently limited to DEC, additional models and tools are likely to be added in the near future (Matzke, pers. comm.)" Should BAYAREALIKE, as I implement it, work with BSM?

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- I'm not clear which model you are trying to BSM under, e.g.:

standard BAYAREALIKE (as in the example script)
or
"BAYAREALIKE+a" (minus d and e), which is basically just a big unordered character model, i.e. Markov-k i.e. Lewis 2001's Mk

Anyways, if many runs fail but some work, just increase max runs to 1000 or something until you get enough successful runs.

If zero runs work, and increasing maxtries even to ridiculous levels doesn't work either -- try hundreds of millions, then you may have hit exactly that issue I put in about the "+a" models.  The +a process wasn't originally programmed in to BSM, I added it later, so it may hit some point in large state spaces where it is just too damn improbable to use BSM's "rejection sampling" approach to get histories.

Since you have BC and BG in the ranges, probably you are just doing standard BAYAREALIKE.  The other question worth asking is: often BAYAREALIKE is the poorest fitting model, which also means it is the model that will have the hardest time producing successful BSMs.  Is there a point to doing BSM except on the better-fitting models?

Cheers!
Nick

Hi -- the script on the validation page doesn't do everything, it's just validating ancestral state probabilities.  In particular, the "simulate_source_areas_ana_clado(res, clado_events_tables, ana_events_tables, areanames)" code is only needed when you want to count events.

Without "simulate_source_areas_ana_clado(res, clado_events_tables, ana_events_tables, areanames)", a BSM knows that this happened:

AB -> ABC

...but it doesn't know if the source area for the dispersal event was "A" or "B".  But, this information is necessary for counting dispersal events, so simulate_source_areas_ana_clado(res, clado_events_tables, ana_events_tables, areanames).

Re: what has to be changed -- use the BSM example script, but run it on a BioGeoBEARS ML analysis that has your distances & areas adjacency files to produce a "res" (or "resDEC" or whatever) results object. Change stratified=TRUE to stratified=FALSE.  That should mostly do it, however, you will have to be patient and figure out other issues that arise (like if you change the name of the results object, you have to change it everywhere it is used), there is no cookbook for custom analyses.

Cheers!
Nick
